items.body:
There's a scene near the end of  Uncut Gems  where the hapless protagonist Howard Ratner, locked behind the security glass of his own shop, watches a parlay come in leg by leg. As each result lands, the magnitude of the one that follows swells, a runaway train of buzz and anxious sweats. Watching Short Span for the past 18 months has felt a lot like standing behind that glass. (Without giving away spoilers, don't worry, that's where the Ratner comparisons end.)

The Sheffield label, run by Matthew Kent—formerly of 2010s-defining mix series  Blowing Up The Workshop —has yet to lose a bet. From Yu Su's  Foundry  to  K Wata 's  Give U Space , each record raises what's staked on the next.  Uuuuuuuu  from Aarhus producer Picture, AKA Natal Zaks is the latest leg to come in—and it's a delight.
 
On the surface, it might seem like an unlikely match. To this day, Zaks is perhaps better known as  Central , who released slinky, midtempo house music as part of Regelbau (he also gave Erika de Casier her  first credit  back in 2017). Short Span, meanwhile, started out a dub techno label two years ago with notable, genre-bending early releases from Sa Pa and Mammo teeing up a widening of the roster in 2026 with the likes of Mr YT and Bot1500. You might consider the label's releases as having little in common musically—instead, the throughline is a disposition rather than a sound. Yu Su  described  Kent as having "all this in-betweenness going on," never settling into one style; Kent has put it similarly himself,  musing  that the label is "for a certain kind of identity that crosses boundaries."

Zaks, then, makes a perfect fit. There's always been something unresolved about his sound, and the traces are audible if you dig: take " Lost Touch ," from 2022's  Up And Down , a twitchy dub techno number built around a wavering synth and a sense of space you'll recognise from the Picture records. 

 Uuuuuuuu  is Zaks' second Short Span record this year, following February's  Eeeeeeee , and harder than the first. "Peeeeeee" (no relation to it's bodily namesake, seemingly) is a claustrophobic techno number with a swinging bassline and an undercurrent of unease like a wonkier Chain Reaction cut. It's reminiscent of being inside a printing factory: the looping synth line is the chug of the machinery, the filter sweep and textures like flying debris, ramping up in the closing minutes, twisting the dial even further on a sense of anxiety. Similarly, "Wooooooo" conjures up the darkest corners of the club. Carrying the air of a closing set on a German mountainside—a rave reshape of Caspar David Friedrich's quintessential painting  Wanderer above the Sea of Fog —wind sweeping around you until a hardgroove bassline introduces an element of steeliness, the summit re-cast in girders and concrete. 

There's also plenty of dubbier, womb-like moments to offset the twitchy mood. Take "Miiiiiii": the pads hold steady but never stop shifting, and beneath them sits what sounds like a springtime field recording, birds chirping into a soft kick drum. "Ziiiiiiiii" has a lighter touch still, like the lovechild of a SnPLO and Dettinger record left out to gather dust—the cycle home from a long night, the melody a hazy sun coming up, the percussion your own worn-out legs chugging you back. "Leeeeee" bridges the two worlds, and gets closer to traditional dub techno than anything else here:  Shinichi Atobe 's warmth over the pure dub glimmer of Vainqueur.

On the dub techno continuum, Picture sits closer to  Convextion  than to most of the '90s set, in both spirit and sound. Whereas Convextion once described his own music as "emotional punishment," on  Uuuuuuuu , I'd suggest Picture hits emotional levity. The material is heavy and the arrangements are crowded, yet the swing keeps everything off the floor: unquantised, the same weight stops pressing down and starts lifting. It's been on  our minds  lately that the 2020s might lack a sound of their own, that the decade has spent itself revisiting other people's halcyon days. Zaks' restless take on dub techno is proof there's still evolution inside the framework, and thrilling stuff still lies ahead.

items.body: Las Instancias comprises Shantala Ferreyra on clarinet, Fermín Suárez on double bass, and Gonzalo Goicoechea on drums. Ferreyra is an Argentinian clarinettist and composer who graduated from the Jazz Performance Program at the Manuel de Falla Conservatory in 2024. In 2025, she released her debut album featuring her original compositions performed by her quintet, and in 2026, she was awarded a scholarship to study composition in Basel, Switzerland. Her work combines composition and improvisation. Suárez is a double bass player, improviser, songwriter, and composer from Rosario, Argentina. His artistic work encompasses a wide range of genres, including jazz, tango, Argentine folk, improvised music, and classical, often mixing, stretching, and breaking the limits between languages and traditions. He co-created the punk-tango and avant-garde ensemble ‘La Rompiente’ for which he composes and arranges. In 2026, he started the solo project ‘Ola de sótano’, a double bass and vocals set with electronics, featuring songs, improvisations and spoken word. He’s also a frequent collaborator of composer and pianist Rocío Giménez López. Goicoechea is a drummer and educator specializing in jazz. He began his studies at the Leopoldo Marechal School of Arts and later continued at the Manuel de Falla Conservatory. Since 2021, he has performed with a variety of jazz-oriented ensembles. After a year devoted to live performance and composition, Las Instancias is released by the Argentine label 625 Discos, and captures the result of their ongoing collaboration so far. With no harmonic instrument, the trio leans into timbre, register, and the register distances between clarinet, bass, and drums. The pared-back format serves as the foundation upon which the group builds its identity and scribes its musical language. The ensemble work their way through various compositions (mostly written by Ferreyra and Suárez) that constantly flirt with the edges of jazz and improvised music, exploring their aesthetic possibilities and different orchestration combinations. Recorded during a session in Rosario, the album seeks to become a living reflection of a live performance, with all its nuances and dynamism. There are fierce solos rooted in jazz language contrasted with moments of introspection expressed through a more abstract idiom, all while maintaining a strong sense of tension and attention. There is a sense of a group whose members perform in proximity, without separation or post-production tricks. The recording is an intimate encounter between both the musicians and the listener. The absence of a harmonic instrument becomes a presence: a framework that pushes them toward inventive orchestration, elastic structures, and an exploration of musical language. This album contains some standout solos and ensemble work. There is a subliminal quality to this trio that makes the music fun, as well as profoundly interesting to listen to. Don’t be fooled by the opening bars of the first track. ‘Lampara Nueva’ starts like a traditional jazz piece, but develops into something extraordinary, the dialogue flowing between the clarinet, bass and percussion like water, flowing back and forth, with a swing here, a change there, and something just for the heck of it anywhere you might care to drop in. There is a taste of traditional jazz, particularly in the drum solos that emerge from the ensemble work, particularly in the second half of the number, but there is also much free playing. ‘Mucho Agora Mismo’ starts with a gentle bass solo and works itself into a frenzy, the clarinet delivering fiery solos across the percussion, with many variations in between. This is a track of many parts, blended seamlessly together. Just beautiful. ‘Dos Veces Agosto’ is a track of harmonies, rhythms, and counter-rhythms, with some bass solos, clarinet that works around the theme, and explores many musical avenues, while maintaining a connection with the central theme. ‘En Meyo’ is a clarinet solo track, with Ferreyra meditating on a theme, while ‘Ok/Off’ is a track where all three instruments lock into the same rhythmic pattern, creating a hypnotic dynamic. A bowed bass emerges, warm and resonant, before the trio returns to their lively, idea‑trading interplay. ‘Pegao’ is introduced by a bowed bass solo, over which the clarinet drops, adding light touches and a rapid change of texture, which the drums enhance, adding their own feel and colour. It is worth listening to this for the changes and rhythmic patterns that evolve, disappear, and re-emerge, led largely by the bass, whose voice is central to this number. The album closes with a second take of 'Mucho agora mismo' which is extravagant and allows each musician to deliver improvised music of the highest calibre. Las Instancias are three musicians whose shared curiosity has shaped a sound that feels both stripped back and richly alive. There’s a cohesion that makes the music both fun and deeply absorbing. You hear three musicians who trust each other enough to take risks — to push, to pull, to leave space, to fill it, to let the music breathe and then ignite. It’s intimate, inventive, and full of personality. Las instancias by Las instancias Get it on vinyl here: https://elasticstage.com/625discos/releases/las-instancias-album Email This BlogThis! items.body: Label: Temperphantom, 2026 Personnel - Victor Vieira-Branco: vibraphone; Sam Yulsman: piano; John Moran: double bass; Joey Sullivan: drums. Playing the vibraphone with a relentless sense of urgency and intent while displaying a strong, distinctive compositional identity, Victor Vieira-Branco is a name to reckon with in contemporary jazz. Rooted in Philadelphia, Bark Culture is Vieira-Branco’s creative brainchild, where intriguing sonic forces feel at once dark and lyrical, sometimes effusive yet always fresh and compelling. For this date, the core trio—with John Moran on double bass and Joey Sullivan on drums—is expanded into a harmonically richer quartet with the addition of pianist Sam Yulsman. The Giant is Awkward , Bark Culture’s sophomore record, opens with “ Palace ”, whose lush theme, rhythmically vivid drive, and hip arrangement command our attention from the very first minute. The bandleader’s rolling liquidity blends seamlessly with sweeping keyboard gestures and the vibrant tangle woven by bass and drums. Sullivan does an intricate, actively propulsive job throughout, fueled by alternative-rock stamina and responsive fills. Yulsman’s “ Farce ”, the only piece not written by Vieira-Branco, is kinetic, asymmetric, and daring in its construction, pervaded by a thrilling sense of uncertainty and a fair dose of arcane postmodern psychedelia. “ Willow ” holds a powerful and consistently engaging backbone that is unafraid of odd meters and metric modulation. Impeccably framed by Yulsman’s off-kilter piano (which sounds great despite being slightly out of tune) and Vieira-Branco’s hallucinogenic vibraphone, the piece climaxes into an unpredictable, stratospheric concentration of sound. On a different register, “ Panic ” gives silence an important role, developing with a balladic feel that favors spacious atmospheres. The album closes with “ Spectrum ”, where the beauty of the instrumentation creates ebbs and flows through intricate accentuation that feels simultaneously startling and exhilarating. There’s space for drum talk before the tension mounts through authoritative bowed bass, nebulous vibraphone streams, dreamy piano sequences, and jittery drumming. With each member focused on injecting energy and emotion, Bark Culture pushes the envelope, reinventing itself as an experimental group that strikes a perfect balance between written material and open improvisation. Vieira-Branco steps forward impressively on The Giant Is Awkward , and it’s remarkable to think these pieces were recorded at the last minute while still in sketch form. Favorite Tracks: 01 - Palace ► 02 - Farce ► 03 - Willow

The race to crown Singapore's next Malay music star is officially on. Anugerah 2026 has unveiled its Top 14 finalists, with the long-running talent competition set to premiere 25 August. The series will air live every Tuesday at 8:30 PM on Suria, mewatch, and Mediacorp Entertainment on YouTube.

Hosted by Fadli Kamsani of Mediacorp RIA 897 and actress Lydia Asyiqin, this year's finalists earned their spots after surviving The Cut — the competition's decisive final audition round. Selected from a pool of 40 hopefuls, the Top 14 impressed judges with their vocal ability, stage presence, and star potential in one of the most competitive stages of the series.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Mediacorp Untukmu (@mediacorp.untukmu)

The finalists come from diverse backgrounds, ranging from students and educators to engineers, entertainers, music teachers, and content creators. Among them are former competition alumni, experienced performers, self-taught vocalists, and rising artistes looking to make their breakthrough on national television. Notable contestants include former K-Pop World Festival Best Vocalist Akif Halqi, singer-songwriter Izzan Adlan, actor Alfan Ryan, and Chariska Diva Anugrah, daughter of Anugerah 2003 champion Eka Mairina. The competition's youngest finalist is 17-year-old Darwish Sofyan, while several contestants are making their television competition debut.

View this post on Instagram

Before stepping onto the live stage, the finalists underwent a series of masterclasses led by industry veterans including Najip Ali, vocal coach Babes Conde, singer Hady Mirza, content creator Zhin Sadali, and Sujadi Siswo. The sessions covered vocal performance, stagecraft, competition strategy, media literacy, social media presence, and personal branding, preparing contestants for the demands of the competition.

Fans can also get a closer look at the contestants through Anugerah: The Cut, a five-part digital-exclusive series that goes behind the scenes of the final audition process and documents the moments that shaped this year's final lineup.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Mediacorp Untukmu (@mediacorp.untukmu)

Viewers will play an active role throughout the competition, with audience votes contributing 20% of each contestant's overall score, while the judges account for the remaining 80%. Voting opens every Wednesday during the live shows, with registered meconnect users able to cast up to 20 votes per day via Mediacorp's voting platform.

The eventual champion will take home the Anugerah 2026 title and a grand prize of $25,000, while the first runner-up will receive $10,000, sponsored by PropNex. A PropNex Special Award worth $5,000 will also be presented to one finalist.

items.body:
Artificial intelligence is no longer just reshaping how music is created — it's also proving to be a lucrative business.

A new study by Kapwing has found that the world's biggest AI music artists have generated an estimated US$6.1 million from more than 2.3 billion combined Spotify streams and YouTube views, underscoring just how quickly AI-generated music is finding mainstream audiences.

The report arrives as streaming platforms continue stepping up efforts to tackle AI-generated content. Spotify has removed millions of AI-generated and spam tracks, while Deezer recently revealed that AI-made songs now account for more than half of all new daily uploads. Despite these measures, the study suggests AI musicians continue to attract millions of listeners and viewers across major platforms.

On Spotify, the top 10 AI artists have collectively earned an estimated US$2.38 million from roughly 595 million streams. Leading the pack is Enlly Blue, a "1950s-style" AI vocalist whose catalogue has amassed 95.2 million streams, translating to an estimated US$380,800 in Spotify earnings.

YouTube paints an even bigger picture. The platform's top 10 AI music creators have generated an estimated US$3.70 million from approximately 1.75 billion views, with Cherry 葵 Nightcore accounting for more than half that figure. The creator has accumulated 941 million views, resulting in estimated earnings of nearly US$2 million.

Beyond revenue, the report highlights the scale of AI artists' reach across streaming services. Masters of Prophecy tops the overall follower rankings with 36.1 million followers across platforms, while King Willonius leads all AI musicians with 500 chart entries. Producer Don Bnnr, meanwhile, boasts the largest playlist reach, appearing on 1,852 playlists with a combined follower count of 46.7 million listeners.

Kapwing compiled the rankings using data from AiMCharts and Songstats, analysing lifetime Spotify streams, YouTube views, followers, playlist placements and chart entries. Estimated Spotify earnings were calculated using an industry-average payout of US$0.004 per stream, while YouTube estimates were based on SocialBlade's default RPM midpoint of US$2.12 per 1,000 views.

As streaming services continue introducing tools to identify and label AI-generated music, the findings suggest that some AI artists have already crossed into the mainstream, building audiences in the tens of millions and generating meaningful revenue despite increasing scrutiny.

Singapore's BLACK ROSE, it's finally happening, The Rose are officially bringing their ROSETOPIA Asia Tour 2026 to the Lion City! The Korean alt-rock outfit will perform at The Star Theatre on 27 October, marking their long-awaited Singapore debut after years of building a devoted global following.

Presented by CK Star Entertainment, the upcoming show will see the four-piece perform fan favourites alongside songs from their upcoming album, giving Singaporean fans their first chance to experience the band's acclaimed live show in person.

Comprised of Woosung, Dojoon, Taegyeom, and Hajoon, The Rose have steadily established themselves as one of Korea's standout live acts with their heartfelt blend of alternative pop, indie rock, and emotionally driven songwriting. Since debuting with 'Sorry', the band has amassed a passionate international fanbase known as BLACK ROSE and more than 1.2 million monthly listeners on Spotify.

Their rise has only accelerated in recent years. DUAL debuted at No. 83 on the Billboard 200, while pre-release single 'Back To Me' has surpassed 92 million streams on Spotify. The band has also become a festival favourite, appearing at Lollapalooza across multiple countries before making history as the first Korean band to perform on Coachella's Outdoor Theatre stage in 2024.

PUMA has teamed up once again with ROSÉ to introduce a graceful new addition to its iconic Speedcat family. The new Speedcat Etoile reimagines the classic motorsport-inspired sneaker with delicate satin-inspired details and a balletcore aesthetic.

The latest silhouette arrives in a soft pastel pink colourway, blending the Speedcat's signature low-profile shape with suede overlays, subtle sheen finishes, tonal branding, and ribbon laces designed to be tied into bows. The result is a feminine take on one of PUMA's most recognisable sneakers, reflecting the continued popularity of ballet-inspired fashion.

Fronted by global K-pop star ROSÉ, the campaign leans into themes of nostalgia and self-expression. The accompanying visuals place the BLACKPINK member among childhood keepsakes and personal mementos, presenting the Speedcat Etoile as a symbol of growth while celebrating individuality and confidence. The campaign's pastel palette represents "every version of you, from where you started to where you're going."

The release also marks another chapter in the resurgence of the Speedcat franchise. Since its return in 2024, the silhouette has evolved through refreshed colourways and new interpretations including the Speedcat Ballet, Speedcat Wedge, Speedcat Mule, and several limited-edition collaborations, helping cement its place as a contemporary streetwear staple.

The Speedcat Etoile will be available from 31 July via PUMA Singapore's online store and selected PUMA retailers.

ENHYPEN and HYBE's original story franchise DARK MOON made their first-ever appearance at San Diego Comic-Con, bringing the group's vampire-inspired universe to one of the world's biggest pop culture conventions through panels, fan events, exclusive merchandise, and immersive experiences.

Held from 23 to 26 July, DARK MOON transformed parts of the San Diego Convention Center into an extension of its fantasy universe, marking a significant step in the franchise's global expansion beyond webcomics and music.

One of the weekend's biggest highlights was Bite Me: Calling All Vampires on 23 July, a panel that explored the enduring appeal of vampire stories across generations. Hosted by TV Guide Magazine's Damian Holbrook, the discussion brought together ENHYPEN, Twilight director Catherine Hardwicke, and actors Peter Facinelli and Ashley Greene. You Yokoyama is back with the next chapter of his solo journey. The SUPER EIGHT member has officially released his sophomore solo album, ROCK FOR YOU, now available to stream worldwide.

Serving as the follow-up to 2025's ROCK TO YOU, the new record marks the evolution of Yokoyama's solo project, which began as what he described as a year-long journey of growth and self-discovery. Earlier this year, the singer hinted at what was to come with a simple message to fans: "I have more to say."

The album arrives after the release of double digital singles 'Pistol' and 'KANJOU MAIGO' in April, as well as sold-out performances at Osaka Castle Hall and Zepp Haneda. Alongside those tracks, ROCK FOR YOU also includes 'Arigato', which Yokoyama debuted live in May, plus six brand-new songs featuring lyrics written by the artist himself.

One of the album's highlights is 'Pudding', a collaboration with fellow SUPER EIGHT member Shota Yasuda, who composed the music for the track. The pair previously worked together on 'cHocolate' and 'Kicyu' from Yokoyama's debut solo album, ROCK TO YOU.

Across the record, Yokoyama continues to channel his personal experiences into heartfelt rock songs, embracing vulnerability while reflecting on the challenges and growth that have shaped both his career and relationship with fans.

Following the album's release, Yokoyama will hit the road for his ROCK FOR YOU LIVE TOUR, beginning 18 August with a 12-city run across Japan.

items.body: Alene. Voldsomt Alene. Alone. Violently Alone. These are the lyrics highlighted by crescendo, volume, and underlined by Karoline Wallace’s celestial voice, in this case, a voice electronically transmuted to sound like Tuvan throat singing, at the apex of Eon’s opening track, “Tycho.” It turns out, much of Eon employs loneliness, separation, and uncertainty as lyrical motifs. But Wallace’s Norwegian text never collapses into isolation. Her opening musings in “Tycho,” named for the famous and complicated Danish astronomer Tycho Brahe, marvel at the distant shining above us, Skapt i vill kraft, created by wild force . So much of the lyrical work by Wallace resounds with interior weather, the cosmos within that counters with enthusiasm the supernovas and aurora borealis without, the fiery and magnetic and kinetic elements of the universe that, like the imagination, contain the power to create and destroy. What does it mean, after all, to be violently alone ? A wild, eternal roar is each being. We are made of star stuff and ultimately whirl in oneness with the most distant corners of the universe. Oneness is never aloneness, and words like buldrer ( roars ), klinger ( rings ), and funkler ( sparkles ) are as present as any other words of emphasis on this astral and exploding album. And the music buoying these lyrics into the electric air is filled with a quiet simmering that always contains the potential to whip and whirl in fiery bursts and detonations at any second. Take, for example, what happens after “Tycho” quietly opens with Karl Bjorå’s sparse albeit off-center guitar strumming. As the music builds to its thunderous Alene crescendo around the 3:30 mark, Martin Langlie begins smacking and slapping the cymbals with increasing excitement. A cello, played by Joel Ring, becomes more obviously audible. And out of the enveloping cosmic atmosphere emerges Signe Emmeluth’s alto saxophone that bursts through the spheres with noise and screaming, as it roars with presence. Emmeluth, it grows apparent, shadows Karoline Wallace’s ethereal vocal line from early on in this work. Only at this explosive point did I become aware of it, however. Wallace’s lonely voice was never alone, it turns out. The album’s second song “Bittelille meg,” or Tiny little me , dances ahead blithely bouncing over a four note ostinato cello line Ring plays with joy and wonder. Tiny little me , listeners are told in Norwegian, lives in a quiet house, but it’s not quiet inside me . “Klokkestein,” follows and calms down all the flaring effusion. Bjorå and Ring play a two note sequence over which Wallace’s vocal lines soar with soothing beauty. This calm interiority is juxtaposed with outward ebullience throughout the entire album. Just listen to the second half of “Klokkestein,” as it shifts into a near house, EDM club track. Or better yet, turn to the wailing opening call of “Atlas,” a high point on the record, as it discharges around the one minute mark its wild energy into the exploding star half of this album always is. The song then proceeds for four minutes oscillating between fire music and the lonely call of evening somnolence, eventually crashing the two states together into one wall of sound. “Karamellgneis,” a meditative work leading to the album’s hushed ending, is marked by up and down tuning and sliding mid-track by Bjorå’s guitar and Ring’s cello, and by Martin Langlie playing the banjo as Wallace reminds us Again and Again Again and Again We were…And we are again And will always be . I have neglected to mention perhaps the core and mantle of Wallace’s project in Eon : geology. On the record’s inner sleeve Wallace writes “In this project, I am inspired by deep time—geological time. An eon is the longest unit of time in the geological timescale.” And, about “Karamellgneis” she writes gneiss “was formed by being pushed beneath the Earth’s crust…The heat and high pressure made it soft as caramel.” I rarely stop to remember that the natural state of rock is also caramel in texture, so accustomed I am to the unyielding formations in which I generally encounter them. But then again, the stars are tiny sparkles on clear evenings in my perception, and not the impossibly giant masses of nuclear fusion they are eons away in outer space. Eon , Wallace’s third album as leader, is a master stroke of musical experimentation and cosmic poetry. Her lyrics and compositions manifest for listeners again and again that all is one, we are never alone, that large is small, quiet is noise, and what is far away is also intimately close. There is no need to feel sad for what has been lost to the past, and to live for anything other than the present moment. But even Wallace's very philosophy culminates in paradox as she ends the record with her father’s words: “It’s easy to say/Live for today,/When I tomorrow/Live for yesterday.” Karoline Wallace’s Eon can be found on Bandcamp: Eon by Karoline Wallace Email This BlogThis! items.body: Label: Trost Records, 2026 Personnel - Otomo Yoshihide: guitar, turntable; Kei Matsumaro: alto and soprano saxophone, electronics. It was hard to connect with this experimental free-jazz duo release by Japanese guitarist Otomo Yoshihide and saxophonist Kei Matsumaro, a native of Palau New Guinea. The album, Shutsumin (a Japanese term referring to the transitional state between sleep and wakefulness, often accompanied by hallucinations and other abnormal sensations), traffics in otherworldly sounds and may well put anyone to sleep, starting with a cold blizzard of cosmic, radioactive pollution that arises from the electronic manipulation of guitar and turntable—emanating torrents of feedback and distorted granularity—alongside piercing, strident saxophone spirals that can be a strain on the ears. Scattered rattling noises and directionless saxophone whirls convey the sensation of standing amid dozens of rusty industrial machines at work. Expect buzzing nuisances, intensifying guitar noise, and heavy, blurring distorted fluxes in a sort of machine language that overwhelms more than it enchants. These fearless explorers take us to uncertain soundworlds charged with labyrinthine, cluttered passages, coordinated overtones, firework-like bursts, and anxious apprehensions. The last three tracks on the album had a more positive effect on me, showcasing a few compelling atmospheres while taking a more substantial and less repetitive, if still abstract, line of action. Folksy melodies begin to surface from Matsumaro’s saxophone over blaring mosaics in the background; cyclic cadences evolve from ambient textures into chaotic clamor before receding into confused murmurs. Things become more interesting and gripping with a stronger harmonic context—thanks to Yoshihide’s hypnotic chords—rather than relying on plain, unceasing buzzing noise. I’m a big fan of Yoshihide’s quintet albums ONJQ Live (2002) and Tails Out (2003), some of his work for Tzadik Records— Flutter (2001) and Dreams (2002)— as well as his inventive, fantastic take on Eric Dolphy’s Out to Lunch (2005). Matsumaro is a new discovery for me. As a duo, they show considerable promise and are unafraid to push the envelope, but ultimately deliver less than expected. Despite its unevenness, Shtsumin may be considered by curious audiophiles with an inclination for sound manipulation. Favorite Tracks: 06 - Utatane ► 07 - Oneiric ► 08 - Meisekimu

items.body:
The biggest names in K-pop are coming together for an ambitious new venture. HYBE, SM Entertainment, JYP Entertainment, and YG Entertainment have announced Fanomenon, a new festival and awards initiative designed to celebrate K-pop and Korean culture on a global scale.

The project will kick off with the Fanomenon Awards, taking place 2–12 December 2027 across Seoul and Goyang. It will then expand overseas with the inaugural Fanomenon Festival in Los Angeles in May 2028, promising a large-scale music experience inspired by festivals like Coachella.

The 11-day awards event will be split across two venues in South Korea. Main performances and ceremonies will be held at Seoul Arena, the country's upcoming 28,000-capacity venue set to open in Chang-dong, while KINTEX in Goyang will host exhibitions, fan activations, and cultural programmes.

Beyond live performances, Fanomenon aims to spotlight the wider Hallyu wave through interactive showcases celebrating Korean food, beauty, fashion, webtoons, films, television, and animation. Organisers also revealed plans to recognise the year's 10 most influential K-pop fan communities during the awards.

The four entertainment giants are establishing a joint venture to lead the initiative, with support from South Korea's Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism. The government said the project is intended to strengthen Korea's cultural influence worldwide while boosting tourism and the country's entertainment industry.

"Korean culture is drawing global attention, and its growth must be sustained and expanded," Culture, Sports and Tourism Minister Chae Hwi-Young said in a statement. "Our primary goal is to make it an event that people around the world want to attend, while earning the trust of the global entertainment industry."

To support the event, the government will assist with immigration procedures, safety management, and international promotion. According to the Korea Culture and Tourism Institute, Fanomenon is expected to attract around 520,000 visitors, including 200,000 international tourists, while generating an estimated 1 trillion won in economic impact.

JYP chief creative officer Park Jin-young also stressed the importance of making the festival financially sustainable, noting that ticket sales and sponsorships will play a key role in supporting the event alongside public funding.

While a full lineup has yet to be announced, Fanomenon marks the first time Korea's "Big Four" entertainment companies have collaborated on a festival of this scale, setting the stage for what could become one of K-pop's biggest global events.

YE (Kanye West) is heading to Indonesia for what is shaping up to be one of Southeast Asia's biggest live music events of the year. The rapper, producer, and fashion icon will perform at YE LIVE IN JAKARTA on 24 October at Gelora Bung Karno (GBK) Main Stadium, marking his first-ever concert in Indonesia and, according to the organiser, his only Southeast Asian stop on his 2026 tour.

Announced by Raw Vision Collective, the show is expected to draw up to 77,000 fans from across the region. The promoter said Jakarta's connectivity, with direct flights from major cities including Singapore, Kuala Lumpur, Bangkok, Manila, Ho Chi Minh City, and Sydney, positions the concert as a destination event for international fans. Official Ticket + Hotel packages will also be available to accommodate visitors travelling into the Indonesian capital.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Raw Vision Collective (@rawvision.collective)

One of the biggest draws of the show is YE's signature Globe Stage production. The immersive 360-degree stage design places audiences around the performance space, creating an experience that blends music, large-scale visuals, and storytelling. The production has become synonymous with YE's recent live shows and will transform GBK Main Stadium into one of the largest concert setups in the region.

"Bringing YE to Jakarta is not only about bringing one of the world's most influential musicians to Indonesia," said Micha Ananda, CEO of Raw Vision Collective. "YE LIVE IN JAKARTA is more than a concert, it's an invitation for fans across Southeast Asia and Australia to experience Jakarta through one unforgettable weekend of world-class live entertainment."

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Raw Vision Collective (@rawvision.collective)

The announcement follows the continued success of YE's latest album, Bully, which debuted at No. 1 on Billboard's Top R&B/Hip-Hop Albums chart. Combined with his reputation for ambitious stage productions, the Jakarta show is expected to be one of the year's most highly anticipated concert events.

Tickets go on sale on 29 July at 10 AM WIB via yejakarta.com, with Loket serving as the official ticketing platform. Entry-tier tickets begin at IDR 1,875,000, while VIP, Super Fans Festival, Royal Suite, and Sky Box options will also be available. Official hotel bundles, which include one night's accommodation at selected hotels near the venue, will be on sale until 29 August, subject to availability.

items.body: Palagoma is not only the first release from Nairobi-based label Cool Waters, it also marks the first time German-born, Kenya-based percussionist Sven Kacirek has collaborated with Ogoya Nengo and Olith Ratengo at the same time. Odd Okoddo, the duo of Kacirek and Ratengo, has been performing since 2018, but with the inclusion of the 83 year old Nengo, a singer from the eastern part of the country, there�s an added traditional depth to the music. A 2025 performance shows Nengo�s lifetime of experience singing Kenya�s dodo tradition around 2 and half minutes in (see below). Furthermore, her inclusion on this album allows her and Ratengo to toss the vocals back and forth as they reference their shared roots (Ratengo and Nengo live minutes from each other). Musically, however, the tracks are driven by Kacirek�s Buchla synth, hand percussion, and occasional kit drumming, which serve to buoy the voices without blotting out the music�s origins. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Bara,� for example, begins with the dime-store thwack of a repeated pattern, a stiff juxtaposition to the voices; yet, as the song rolls along, a 4/4 clink appears, then a burbling bass, and finally, what sounds like a xylophone. Layers of synthesized polyrhythms keep presenting themselves with a subtlety almost unnoticeable, until, by the track�s end, it feels organic, as if it�s all been underneath the two voices all along. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Sarah,� perhaps the album�s most intense track, features a lead vocal from Ratengo and tentative, percussive spittles from Kacirek. And while the technology never tries to overtake the vocals, it does sneak up and punctuate the track�s urgency, as edgy distortion sneaks in here and there just as Ratengo�s voice reaches its peak. The term �folktronica� has been bandied about as a way to house the type of music on offer here. In fact, exploratory collaborations such as Chouk Bwa & The �ngstr�mers as well as much of Kampala, Uganda�s Nyege Nyege label house sounds that might be �folktronic� in some way. What�s more interesting and important about this music, though, is how truly global so much of it is while maintaining a deep connection to Africa and its diasporic communities. The music on Palagoma , as well as much of what�s linked above (and available in countless other recent recordings) demonstrates a real willingness for cultures to respond to each other without trampling traditions altogether. Instead, roots become avant-garde and innovations become seemingly thousands of years old. Certainly the inclusion of an 83 year old traditional Kenyan singer only recently making her global debut as she tours with a duo whose instrumental voice is a white male saturated in electronic Kenyan rhythms demonstrates this blurring. The music this trio makes is certainly of the 21st century, but it�s often hazy, sparse, and open, keeping it from a quick sell-by date or confining it to a specific genre. Instead, it�s a beautiful example music as grace.

According to its founder, Eugene Rodriguez, who also sings and plays on the record, Los Cenzontles is a �musical group and non-profit organization, which I founded over thirty years ago.�  As he continues in the album�s liner notes, the group �has a long history of producing projects exploring Mexico�s deep roots and our connections with various traditions that, so far, have included Irish, Louisiana Creole, Cuban, American cowboy, classical, pop, rock, and blues�, the latest of which is
Adios Ke Aloha: Waves of the Same Sea
. Los Cenzontles translates to the mockingbird, or, from its Aztec root word, the bird of four hundred voices. This is a fitting name for the range of musical diversity represented here.
With songs sung in Spanish, Hawaiian, and English, the concept traces back to the legacy of Mexican cowboys who travelled from California to the Hawaiian Islands to wrangle the long-horned cattle introduced there in the nineteenth century. They also brought the guitar. The 16 tracks feature old Hawaiian songs with new Spanish lyrics, old Mexican songs with new Hawaiian lyrics, new compositions, and traditional Americana. Yet it is an entirely cohesive musical package held together by dense arrangements of ukuleles, guitars, Mexican harp, and accordion.
Sonny Lim & David Hidalgo
Besides their distinctive voices, the headline artists Taj Mahal and David Hidalgo provide the gravitas and musicianship that their long and distinguished careers have earned. According to the liner notes, they were the catalysts behind the project and facilitated the choice of songs, arrangements, and played a range of instruments. On vocals they are joined by Hawaiian natives Gary Haleamau, Sheldeen Haleamau, Sonny Lim, and long-time Cenzontles member Fabiola Trujillo.
Deportee
To give a taste of the sessions, included before the traditional �Fishin� Blues� is Taj Mahal teaching the musicians how to play it. Sung by David Hildalgo,  the lovely �A Matter of Time� comes from the 1984 album
Will the Wolf Survive
by his most famous project, Los Lobos. Another standout for me, �Navegar� features a slack string guitar solo reminiscent of Duane Eddie and one of many tasty lap steel turns by Sonny Lim. Their interpretation of Woody Guthrie's �Deportee� moves into social commentary, highlighting the cruel realities of being a migrant worker in America.
Vaquero Paniolo
Recorded over five days, mostly live in one room at the Los Cenzontles headquarters in San Pablo, California, including the talents of some of their academy�s students, the recording has real spontaneity to it. Arrangements are stretched by improvisations, sometimes by several different instruments on a single tune. The project also represents a great spirit of cooperation and diversity of language, culture, age, and gender. It includes the inputs of musical legends, seasoned pros, and amateurs. The wonderfully rich and often stereotyped musical cultures of both Mexico and Hawaii are represented here with the authenticity of lived experience.
Adios Ke Aloha: Waves of the Same Sea
is a worthy addition to Los Cenzontles� important work. Quoting Rodriguez again, �Culture is a fabric within which we are all woven.�

Kalaniemi is a lovingly melodic accordion player, with a sharp ear for a good tune, building each one into a thing of great beauty, while pianist Alakotila not only supports her but adds enough of his own to help transform every piece into a glistening gem.
There�s a sense of calmness to the work here, a long, sweet exhalation between two instrumentalists who are deep enough in sync to allow seamless improvisation beyond any written score and carry the listeners along with them. For much of the album, it�s just the pair of them, including Kalaniemi�s wordless voice, as on the opener, the tradional �Lyck�nskan.� She does charmingly sing lyrics on the title track, written by Lasse M�rtenson, with the sound there neatly and sparingly expanded with the addition of a string quartet.
Morgondimma

Yet, what makes this music so fascinating in general, that is, beyond its unswerving ability to fill dance floors, is the fact that these two islands, part of the Paises Africanos de Lingua Oficial Portuguesa (PALOP) regions of the world, are the second smallest African country; Seychelles is smaller. There are only 12 villages on Sao Tom�, lots of rain forest and, not surprisingly, lots of rain. I mention this because one could be fooled into thinking, with music like what�s on offer here, there must have been a music scene larger than there actually was. Not that little was happening, but that less got recorded or released than it might have had there been a city such as Lagos or Nairobi with the studios, labels, and pressing plants to better document it all. The music here, like Volume 1- recorded during Africa�s so-called golden age- is known as Puxa, a complex stew of ingredients from other former African Portuguese colonies mixed with rhythms that, with the help of dancers, can summon spirits or exorcise demons. At least according to some. It�s worth knowing that a 100 years or so ago, the Portuguese banned Puxa dance; it�s also worth knowing they appear to have failed miserably at this silly endeavor. Tucked away in modern Puxa is merengue, Kompas, Soukouss, Benga, and much else. One suspects much of this is coincidental, while other grooves were definitely imported considering both Portuguese rule and the islands� location over the Atlantic from the Caribbean. But don�t be fooled into thinking these two islands don�t have their own thing, as the sounds on this collection show. L�VE L�VE Vol. 2: Sao Tom� & Principe Sounds 70s-80s - Pedro Lima Pedro Lima, who has featured in his own Bongo Joe collection, leads a fiery band, complete with choked guitar vamps tussling with a kit drummer as a lead guitar comments from the sidelines on �Sossegado.� Elsewhere, Sangazuza demonstrates what happens when the bass and keys drop out, leaving the drummers and guitars to ride out a groove and drive dancers mad in the process. In collaboration with avant-garde composer and filmmaker Francesco Paolo Paladino, and poet and music writer Luca Chino Ferrari, Songs of Compassion is eleven songs containing subversive and at times beautiful music, and richly evocative lyrics. Francesco Paolo Paladino and Luca Chino Ferrari | Photo by Maria Assunta Karini Songs of Compassion has two challenges for the listener. The first is the music, called variously avant-garde, ambient, modal, non-linear, and a few more. It is played mostly on pianos mixed in and out of the foreground, sometimes doubled, and sometimes out of phase, joined by strings, woodwinds, synth washes, and steely sounds. Initially disorienting, the music serves to remind us how locked our minds are to Western notions of harmonic movement. It speaks of alternative musical narratives much older and much further away. They are songs that subvert the song: more like Steve Reich than Steve Stills; more like Phillip Glass than Phil Collins. UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY - Pale Wanderer At the same time, there are the poetic yet strikingly contemporary lyrics. �Pale Wanderer� talks about the fact that authoritarianism needs willing accomplices, describing what happens �When you make a deal with darkness.� UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY (Dorothy Moskowitz, Francesco Paolo Paladino e Luka Chino Ferrari) by Silentes �Charlottesville� (written with the late Joe Byrd) evokes the time not long ago when torch-wielding nazis, proud of the metaphoric Ns on their tunics, chanted the antisemitic tropes paraphrased in Moskowitz�s words, �We�ll be one people, pure of race/No greedy throng could take our place� . Besides the overtly political lyrics, in the tradition of 1960s protest songs, there are also thoughtful meditations on mortality and our place in the universe. The message is high-minded yet sincere and direct. World weary and wise, Moskowitz�s voice inhabits the evocative philosophical lyrics with the authority of a skilled method actor. The melodies unfold like streams of consciousness, rising and falling, not following expected diatonic chord progressions, but honouring, instead, the value of each word. Moskowitz�s piano acts as another voice and sometimes a kind of Greek chorus commenting on the proceedings. The surrounding music frames, creates pulses and dissonances, and shimmers. The return of Dorothy Moskowitz with her renamed project has arrived in a moment quite similar to the times that spawned its predecessor. Political division, unrest, and uncertainty always generate artistic reaction, and United States of Alchemy roared back to life with their epic 24-minute opening track �Under an Endless Sky� in 2023, serving perhaps as an �In-A-Gadda-Da-Vida� for our times. Songs of Compassion continues to challenge how we think about our world. It�s music that defies the song form, while doing exactly what music is supposed to do�enrich the human condition. items.body: Those of us who have been digging into Analog Africa�s increasingly formidable releases over the last two decades are well aware of the massive amount of raw, vodun-based Sato and Sakpata-derived funk the label has issued by Benin�s most prolific 1970s-era band, the Orchestre Poly-Ritmo. AA has dropped no fewer than 3 compilations of their heaviest material, as well as a reissue of the band�s first LP, in an effort to give them the international status they deserve. That being said, what might be different about this collection of their music? And who is Antoine Dougb�? Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa As it turns out, Dougb� was a song-conjurer whose mode of musical transfer was slapping his legs in a rhythm known as Cavacha, a groove created by drummer Belobi Meridjo, who was inspired by a train cadence that he worked into a pattern that ultimately spread like a 21st century California wildfire throughout Congolese pop music in the mid-1970s. Dougb�, known as the �Devil�s Prime Minister,� was also a practitioner of vodun who inspired fear in any musician he felt was unsuited to play his music, which is how he landed on working exclusively Poly-Ritmo, as he felt they could nail what he wanted in ways other bands couldn�t. His recording career was brief - 3 albums and a few singles - but as this collection shows, it was potent. Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa Because of the era from which this music dates, it�s not surprising that the recording and instrument tones have changed - the guitars have a plastic sheen and synthesizers appear- even if the music remains rooted in the 1970s. Perhaps the influence of the Cuban son is more apparent here than on other Poly-Ritmo collections, especially in the collection�s initial offerings. And yes, Congolese rumba, then shaking all of sub-Saharan Africa to its knees, is present too. �Ma Won Min Towe Leo� is one example. Opening with a bed of synthesizers, the shimmering guitars, tinny, seemingly squeezed dry by the 80s themselves, lock in over relentless high-hat-focused grooves. The guitars finally start firing in different directions midway through, before that synth weaves back in, forming a bed underneath it all. Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa �We Tayi Sin Assi Tche� is much more overtly Cuban. With its insistent cowbell, classic, nasal vocal call and response, and tight, repeated guitar figures, its debt to mid-twentieth century Afro-Cuban sons is transparent. Another track, �Djomido Ma Dougbe Tche� rides a groove reminiscent of 70�s-era Franco classic �Liberte.� The pulse is relentless, and the guitar solo repeats a tight repetition of a few notes, driving listeners to ecstasy all the while. However, none of this music is a mere copy of its influences; rather, like so much potent pop coming from the continent at the time, it is a swirl of major influences rendered by local rhythms and vocal phrasing to give it specific identity, in this case, to Benin. Dougb�s musical role on this collection is a bit murky. One of his three albums has a photo of him, fully mic�d behind a collection of hand drums, so perhaps he served as a percussionist/vocalist; this release never explains. He wasn�t a songwriter in the traditional sense. It seems he was more of an instigator and arranger, but his thumbprint was apparently heavy enough to warrant his name on the records he was involved with. Whatever the case, in his brief run as a recording artist, he and Poly-Ritmo produced a handful of driving, Cavacha-inspired grooves that can still wear holes in club floors. items.body: Tako Toki are like desert island musicians who, castaway without their instruments, were forced to construct their own. Lucky for us, they are as skilled in making instruments as they are in creating original songs with which to show off their handicrafts. Un Dimanche � Monaco is the band�s follow-up to their well-received debut, Hirsute Farfelus , with a similar mash of musical styles. Before discussing the music, we need to talk about their instrument closet. They really have built everything they play out of bric-a-brac, odds and ends, and rubbish. I�m not sure from listening which is which, but they call their instruments, in an incomplete list, tassofons, tilofons, and tubofones, clarinuts, didjerimou, and klarbass, and my favorite, kitchenofon. (I will refer to what I hear by the names of store-bought instruments that they sound like.) The most surprising thing for me was how accurate the instruments were to pitch and how good they sounded under the harsh scrutiny of modern recording microphones that have documented a rich, high-quality sound. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki They have also very effectively matched their choice of instruments with the style of music that inspires their compositions. Right off the top, �Yinitza� features a laughing clarinet singing a klezmer tune accompanied by bassoon for the bass, frantic two-time percussion, and the exuberant human yelps found on many klezmer recordings. As on this track, many tunes feature improvisations that show an impressive degree of musicianship. On the cumbia-inspired �Le Cuenta,� the characteristic flute carries the tune, augmented by a Spanish singing chorus, and remarkably rich-sounding Latin percussion. The title track surrounds us with afrobeat woodblocks, shakers, and rattles scattered around the mix. The melody is played on a marimba ornamented with bells and cymbals. Again, the lead player improvises over the tune and often against the beat with jazzy chops. The flute returns on the samba-inspired �Ambiguidade,� and on �Aksum� it traces a trance-like Middle Eastern tune reminiscent of a 60s TV spy-show theme. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki Full of fun and one of a kind, Un Dimanche � Monaco celebrates our universal love of rhythmic, melodic, and harmonic sounds and the varied, wonderful ways cultures have organized that love in what we call music. At the same time, playing on literal pieces of junk, Tako Tiko reminds us, as we contemplate many mall music shops filled with gleaming wood and brass instruments and countless unused guitars lying in closets, that musicians will always find a way to make music. Tiny Sun creates tiny songs that give off light and heat well out of proportion to their size. Composed, performed, and produced by Martina Sorbara, Jonathan Goldsmith, and Don Rooke, the record is vaguely Americana, with plucked guitars and ukuleles, chiming keyboards, and the lonesome slide of the guitar.
Vanishment
contains eighteen sparkling miniatures - that take a scant 34 minutes to negotiate - notable for their economy of arrangement and the subtle directness of the lyrics. The tracks glow with Martina�s clear, high, and sometimes fragile voice.
The songs are about loss: lost love, lost confidence, but sometimes about resignation to the enigmatic quirks of the world. The tone of wry fatalism mirrors the fact that this project is the work of many years of collaboration and email exchanges while the trio pursued their musical day jobs. Jonathan Goldsmith is an award-winning composer for television and film, Don Rooke fronts the Toronto roots band The Henrys, and Martina Sorbara is known for folk, electropop, and her band Dragonette.
Kerosene Madrigal
The range of backgrounds leads to many styles, and the record betrays interesting influences. The opening track, �Kerosene Madrigal,� is a sort of miner�s blues reminiscent of Michelle Shocked. The soul-country of �Imagined Love� reminded me of fellow Torontonians Cowboy Junkies, especially the sweet organ. The stoic and twangy �Don�t Fault the Stars for Falling� could have been a Dolly Parton tune.
A Grand Expanse
�A Grand Expanse� has a more ambitious arrangement.  It sounds like the end-credits song from a long-ago film we only vaguely remember. It says everything it needs to in one minute and twenty seconds and exactly 38 words. It is quintessential Tiny Sun.
The entire recording feels like music from a dream, and since no one knows exactly what dream music sounds like, this could be it.

items.body: In August 1819, tens of thousands of working men and women gathered in St. Peter�s Field in Manchester to hear the politician Henry Hunt speak. They were difficult times, many still out of work after the Napoleonic wars, rising prices and low wages � and always those at the bottom of the heap suffering. Hunt was a famed orator, a man on the side of the people, able to stir and inspire with his voice. Although the gathering was peaceful, the size of the crowd terrified the magistrates, who panicked and imagined an uprising. They sent in half-trained dragoons and the cavalry, who rode down, slashed and killed without compunction or compassion. In the end, 18 died and up to 700 were wounded. It was a stain on the nation, an outrage; prompting Percy Shelley, one of the poetic giants of the age, to write The Masque of Anarchy , with its famous lines: �Rise like Lions after slumber / in unvanquishable number / She your chains to earth like dew / Which in sleep had fallen on you / Ye are many - they are few.� Peterloo, as people called it, remains one of the seminal events in English working-class history, one that Sean Cooney of the Young 'Uns has revisited for this album of original songs, which is lavishly presented in a book with contemporary letters, political cartoons and illustrations to create a multimedia event. It�s ambitious, no doubt about that, and he�s selected some great talent to help � guitarist Sam Carter, the almost ubiquitous fiddler/singer Eliza Carthy, Ben Nicholls supplying background and texture on various instruments, and the Lancashire industrial ballad singer Jennifer Reid, who doubles as narrator. Peter's Field by Sean Cooney, Eliza Carthy, Sam Carter, Jennifer Reid For a small ensemble, they make a powerful noise. The songs capture the feel of the day; the anticipation and excitement at the summer gathering, the joy that turns to terror and flight as the troops charge, then the bitter, mournful aftermath, voiced some powerful melodies and very well-chosen images. As a writer, Cooney often focuses on the personal in the small tales of people like �Sam Bamford� and �Mary Fildes,� while the three short pieces that comprise �The Monkey Rides The Mare� capture the bluster and arrogance of the soldiers. Peter's Field by Sean Cooney, Eliza Carthy, Sam Carter, Jennifer Reid Cooney is a persuasive singer, and on this heartfelt project, he puts plenty of emotion into his voice. Having two other outstanding vocalists alongside him makes for a wonderful triple threat. In these days when governments across the world are cracking down on protest, this stands as a sobering and very timely reminder. It�s a history lesson, yes, but the detail of the history stays in the book, while the music creates a set of songs that will resonate and remain for a long time. Find the artist online. A striking UNESCO-designated World Heritage Site set, the Loreley is a slate pinnacle on a mythic horseshoe bend of the Rhine River, memorializing an enduring German literary legend both tragic and romantic. The setting is thus well-suited for Mac�s mystical spirit and lyrical style. By this stage of his career, he characterized his live show as a Mardi Gras revue with a mix of New Orleans standards and some of his most recognizable compositions.
Hence, he opens with the NOLA classic �Iko, Iko,� a half-sung, half-chanted celebration of community participation in the renowned Mardi Gras second-line street procession. Then comes the in-your-face boast �Qualified,� wherein the singer warns, �I got the power to control / I can see clean through you, blind mole / I want to tell you now, I'm qualified / You know that I'm qualified.�
Any Dr. John fan will recognize �I Walk on Guilded Splinters,� a moody, percussively insistent, foreboding expression of the Night Tripper�s immersion in �funknology� (his term), gris-gris herbology, and hoodoo incantation, punctuated with jungle growls and cries, a loopy, spooky slide whistle, and an extended psych-guitar solo: �Walk thru the fire / Fly thru the smoke / See my enemy / At the end of dey rope.�
Every piece in this well- honed set deserves considertion. Although Dr John lived for many years in Los Angeles and New York, his enduring hometown connection shows in the fond inclusion of his own �Sweet Home New Orleans� and �Goin� Back to New Orleans,� and he nods to a key influence with a funky rendering of Duke Ellington�s �I'm Gonna Go Fishin�.� Among other gems are Mac�s Top�10 hit �Right Place, Wrong Time,� and the instantly recognizable closer, Earl King�s �Big Chief,� another Mardi Gras burner.
Regarding his live performance approach, per the notes, �I always play a little bit of everything. I think that�s what music�s about: a little bit of somethin� old, somethin� in the middle, somethin� new, and somethin� as yet uncreated.�
Dr John's�s longtime fans will welcome this archival gem, which also is a solid introduction for any late comers to the party. Surmounting the barriers of language and culture, the power of
At the Rockpalast
is also evident in the enthusiastic audience response. As he declares, �If you�re gonna get off on somethin� you don�t need to know nothin� about it. Music is a universal language.�

items.body: Kr�ta , the latest release on Norway's Taragot label, features a Swede and two Norwegians playing interpretations of mainly traditional tunes from their respective countries. Fiddler Mats Ed�n has long been involved in Swedish folk music, as a player, composer and teacher, and in the process exploring and integrating different musical styles and approaches. Tellef Kvifte was in the pioneering Norwegian crossover band Slinkombas in the 1970s and has continued to play a central role in Norwegian folk music, both as a musician and an academic. Most often heard playing the sj�fl�yte , more widely known as a recorder, Kvifte has employed other instruments from outside the Norwegian tradition, in particular the saxophone and bagpipes. His son Knut Kvifte Nesheim , a drummer and composer, has also shown a determination to blur the lines between different musical genres, both in his solo and group projects. Kr�ta by Ed�n/Kvifte/Nesheim trio It comes as no surprise then to find this trio offering a far from conventional take on the tunes they have chosen. While dance tunes may be the source of most of the material here, this feels more akin to chamber music; not that it is remotely classical in style, but in the sense it conveys of three players engrossed in a musically intimate conversation. This is not a performance appropriate for accompanying dancers but might instead be seen as an exploration of hidden possibilities of meaning in the music. In so doing it reveals some of its underlying mystery, including, perhaps, a darker side. Just as in an Ibsen play, where the surface bonhomie, jollity and social nicety can be hiding something more sinister, in Scandinavian dance music there are at times hints of a troublesome undercurrent below the surface. So the decision to open proceedings with �Fossgrimen,� a fiddle tune from Norway's Setesdal valley, is perhaps significant. A fossgrimen is a mythical creature, a kind of water-sprite living in waterfalls from whom fiddle-players were considered to have learned their skills and for that were not universally welcomed, with the fiddle considered to be the devil's instrument. Kr�ta by Ed�n/Kvifte/Nesheim trio Tellef Kvifte takes the lead melody on most tracks but on the Swedish �Polska from Per Myhr,� having played a repeated introductory riff on the sj�fl�yte, with Mats Ed�n providing an amorphous textural accompaniment below and Nesheim adding some quiet tinkling, it's Ed�n who introduces the tune on the fiddle with Kvifte proceeding to play in unison. It's a short track and almost as soon as it gets going things start to fragment and everything grind to a halt.

items.body: Sendas by Omar Sosa True to a Monk-inspired commitment never to play the same thing twice, Cuban pianist and composer Omar Sosa�s Sendas (Pathways), his latest solo offering, is the vivid invention of a pensive, restlessly creative, evolutionary artistry. As with all Sosa�s work, Sendas is the fortunate product of serendipity. In 2021 the COVID lockdown was underway, his marriage was ending, and a scheduled Milan appearance cancellation garnered an invitation to record at the Fazioli Pianoforti Concert Hall, annex to the renowned Italian piano manufactory in Sacile, Pordenone, about an hour northeast of Venice. At Fazioli, Sosa found himself in august company. Herbie Hancock and a host of classical pianists are Fazioli artists. Among the institutions that have embraced the Fazioli sound are the Juilliard School, Teatro La Fenice (Venice), the Budapest Palace of Arts, the Paris Conservatory, the Beijing Grand Theatre, and the universities of Salzburg, Graz, and Vienna. An unscripted two-hour solo improvisation on a Fazioli grand in the empty concert hall provided the raw audio for Sendas , later to be flavored in the mix, sparsely, with voice clips, percussion, loops, field recordings, found sounds effects that Sosa has collected over a career spanning four decades. As Sosa related to me soon after completing the post-production of Sendas , �Humanity is spiritually lost. We humans are all in this together. We need to evolve, but always keeping the traditions, walking with a strong, determined pace. We need more grounded music with overtones that resonate with the lower chakras� like throat singing, a mantra of the universal music.� �Creativity is about combining all your influences in a new way. I don�t aspire to be jazz, Latin, timba, reggaeton, classical. I avoid styles, but I respect the forms.� �I try not to think about how listeners will receive it but I do try to address their expectations, and go with the music to some other new place. Many free spirits come to listen, to be a part of the journey we are on.� Sosa laughs, �My son says, �Your niche is really small.� But the people who come really are there to be part of what we are going to do.� �Economics, technology, the streaming ear wash, algorithms all want to put you into a defined category � and so do many music journalists! The industry�s mentality is that any investment in artists must be defined by market categories to be profitable.� �But I play to be free of that,� Sosa says. �I play without thinking. There are no wrong notes. I love the first take. That�s the take, the natural voice of your soul. �Less is more� is a mantra in my life and music.� Consider the opening of �Inside the Spirit,� easing in leisurely, reaching over the keyboard into the resonant heart of the instrument, plucking and stroking the strings, teasing out a fuller resonance � only later to be embellished in the studio mix with light percussion and the muted Spanish-language refrain of a pregonero or street vendor, as might be heard in the calles of Havana or any other Latin American barrio. Sendas by Omar Sosa Moving from the secular to the sacred, �Deities Serenade� is an Afro-Cuban invocation of the shape-shifting divine, yet with ample room for ecumenical recasting in accord with a listener�s own self-location. �Inside My Soul� and �Something from Home� are Sosa works that to my ear may be an intuitive response to the distant call of Chopin�s "Nocturnes," to which Sosa says he listened every night for two years as a conservatory student in Cuba. Sendas by Omar Sosa �Caribbean Movement� and �Shirma� speak to Sosa�s rootedness in the lyrical, rhythmic, and harmonic heritage of the plantation islands where African and European cultures tragically entwined. In the violent forging of the world�s first truly modern people, social, cultural, linguistic, and musical displacements proved more flexible and accommodating than many of those same people, who shaped a contentious convergence of traditions into a changing same that persists into the unfolding present, ever yet to come. With expressive transcendence such as this, seeking to reduce the spiritual essence and inspiration of Sosa�s music to words is rather a fool�s errand. Better rather to listen, to contemplate, to perceive the pathway, to wander the sonic sendas coursing to the next way station without prejudice or preconception. To that end, Scott Price, Sosa�s longtime manager and friend relates, �We are using Sendas as the springboard for our first experiments in AI-generated Omar Sosa music videos.� Absent the opportunity to see and hear Sosa perform live, the palpable ideal, these ancillary audiovisual experiments further the ineffability of his artistic quest, the unique nature of the listening experience and all that ensues.

items.body: Editor's note: When this set of recordings came to me, I was at a loss as to how to share it. It's not music, in any traditional sense (although there is some freestyle rapping), and a 'review' of such an artifact of reality seems superfluous to the content. Instead, I asked sound recordist Ian Brennan if I could simply use his own brief commentary and the recordings he made on the street in Chicago. Twenty-five people afflicted by gun violence participated, many from the very block we�d setup on. Many neighbors were pulled-in spontaneously. Almost every one in the community had been impacted by violence somehow� both on the receiving and the inflicting end, and many both. One woman had just come from a memorial service, another was on her way. That�s how far-reaching the violence. Almost no one went untouched. The Forgotten Parts by Chicago Gunfire Survivors By chance, we convened on the day that Trump ordered the deployment of the National Guard to the city. The recording took place on the front porch of the leader's ninety-four-year-old grandmother's house�right in the heart of the ��hood,� beneath the Midway Airport�s landing path. A pair of stray pitfalls stalked the block. But the grandmother warned not of gunshots, but the mosquitoes in her yard. The Forgotten Parts by Chicago Gunfire Survivors We were in a section of town that one man defined as �the forgotten parts.� Just a short jaunt from the designer clothes shops and posh hotels of the city�s Magnificent Mile, the Southside spawned such legendary Blues artists as Muddy Waters, Willie Dixon, and Howlin� Wolf. Jazz musicians like Lionel Hampton and even Benny Goodman, hailed from nearby. The Forgotten Parts by Chicago Gunfire Survivors The participants ranged in age from seventeen to sixty-seven, but the pattern held true. The person who�d asserted �you�ll really want to hear my story,� was the least compelling. The reluctant, the most moving. One elder�s tough facade broke down as she shared how she�d lost both her sons. She tearfully apologized, �I�m sorry. I�m sorry. I�m sorry.� But she had nothing to be sorry for. Society is the one that owes the apology� for the staggering statistical inequities of which no reasonable defense can be made. The Forgotten Parts by Chicago Gunfire Survivors Editor's note: The full set of recordings are available on Bandcamp. Any profits from this project will be donated to Cure Violence Global , who states that their mission is "advancing an evidence-based health approach to end violence globally." When I asked him about the background sounds, producer Ian Brennan added, "No music is added. It�s all sounds from the source environment. I also ran loops/drones on a different track in the background as they spoke, and when they ended up being incidentally/somewhat magically/eerily synchronous, that is what was used for a few pieces with 'accompaniment' like some of the rap freestyles."
